subject: Biology
title: Tears and Saliva: Chemical Defenders
description: A quick win: understand Tears and Saliva: Chemical Defenders.

hook.text: Every time you blink, your tears wash away bacteria and destroy them with an enzyme called lysozyme.

buildup.text: Lysozyme breaks down bacterial cell walls. It's found in tears, saliva, and nasal secretions.

discovery.text: Alexander Fleming discovered lysozyme in 1922 when his own nasal mucus killed bacteria on a petri dish.

twist.text: Fleming later discovered penicillin—but he called lysozyme his more important finding.

climax.text: Your body runs chemical warfare 24/7. Every fluid that exits your body carries antimicrobial agents.

punchline.text: Your tears don't just cry. They kill.

details.summary: Tears and saliva contain lysozyme, an enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls, along with antibodies and other antimicrobial proteins. These secretions continuously wash and chemically defend exposed surfaces like the eyes and mouth against microbial invasion.
details.whyItMatters: Eyes and mouth are critical entry points for pathogens. The antimicrobial properties of tears and saliva explain why eye infections are relatively rare despite constant exposure, and why dry mouth significantly increases infection and tooth decay...
takeaways: Lysozyme in tears and saliva destroys bacteria by breaking cell walls
Secretory IgA antibodies in saliva neutralize pathogens on mucosal surfaces
Continuous secretion provides constant chemical defense at vulnerable openings

faq.question: Why does dry mouth increase the risk of tooth decay?
faq.answer: Saliva contains antibacterial enzymes, antibodies, and minerals that suppress harmful bacteria and remineralize tooth enamel. Without adequate saliva flow, bacterial populations grow unchecked, acid production increases, and teeth lose their protective mineral coating.

faq.question: How effective is lysozyme at killing bacteria?
faq.answer: Alexander Fleming discovered lysozyme before penicillin and found it could kill many common bacteria within minutes by cleaving peptidoglycan in their cell walls. It is most effective against gram-positive bacteria and provides a constant baseline defense in tears, saliva, and nasal secretions.
